prize_parts.citation: for the invention of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, and for their realization at the 10^-18 level of accuracy

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single part, B009, credited to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. The case rests on one separable idea and one demonstrated frontier. Katori's magic-wavelength condition removes the lattice light shift that would otherwise forbid trapping atoms for spectroscopy, and his first strontium demonstration showed that very many atoms can be interrogated at once. Ye's group then showed that this architecture reaches fractional uncertainty near 1e-18 and operates in a many-body-aware regime. Independent strontium and ytterbium laboratories reproduce the result, and clock comparisons already use it. On the chair's question about invention versus discovery, I read the criterion as 'discovery or invention', and I take it as a statement about the person responsible for a new principle. Magic-wavelength trapping is a principle, not an incremental refinement of an existing instrument; the 2005 comb prize honoured the means of counting optical cycles and the 2012 prize honoured control of single trapped ions, and neither covers confining a large neutral ensemble without perturbing the transition. On the citation, I now prefer to name both the principle and the accuracy frontier, because the first-round exchange showed that my earlier wording dropped the part of the work that is credited to Ye. The citation states what it credits and so leaves out, by omission, the other Sr, Yb and Hg groups, the ion clocks and the comb lineage.
statement.case_against: The reservations from round 1 remain, and the exchange has not removed them. Optical clocks are metrology, and a critic can read the prize as a third award in one lineage after 2005 and 2012. Two names compress a history that includes Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lisdat and the PTB and NIST groups, and a citation can narrow the claim but cannot give those groups credit. Seven of the eight round-1 files, including mine, cite concrete uses that are partly prospective (dark-matter couplings, geodesy, the redefinition of the second). Danielsson is right that the clocks have not yet produced a fundamental-physics result of their own, so the justification is the invention and its reproduction, not a delivered discovery about nature. I also recognise that unanimity in round 1 owes something to members moving after the opening ballots, so it should not be treated as evidence of scientific weight.

responses.point: Danielsson accepts B009 as the one candidate where scientific, attribution and maturity arguments align, but warns that eight rankings and six top-three placements show a safe consensus pick, and that the clocks have not yet produced a fundamental-physics result of their own.
responses.response: I accept the warning and I do not rest my case on the count of rankings. My basis is that Katori's magic-wavelength idea is a specific principle that had to be conceived and then shown to work, and that Ye's group established that it delivers 1e-18. I agree that a delivered fundamental-physics result is absent, so I would not cite dark matter or constant variation as the achievement; those are consequences the committee may note at most. If the committee wants the prize to turn on a result about nature, I would send it to B018 before B009, but that is a different criterion from the one in the will as I read it, which allows an invention.

responses.point: Kroll's strongest reservation is that 2005 and 2012 already cover the neighbouring lineage so a clock prize looks like a third helping, and he prefers to wait if the redefinition of the second is the real outcome; he also discloses his Boulder connection to the Hall laboratory.
responses.response: On the lineage point I disagree in part: the comb is a ruler for optical frequency and the trapped ion is a single quantum system, whereas the lattice clock is about interrogating a large neutral ensemble without perturbing it, so the physics is separate even where the laboratories overlap. On timing, I would not wait. The redefinition is a metrological decision made by a standards body, and a prize for the invention does not depend on its outcome; waiting for it would tie a physics award to a policy process. On Kroll's disclosure, I think recording it is sufficient, since he has no stake in the outcome and a doctoral-era visit to a laboratory in Boulder is not a collaboration with either credited name. I would ask him to say if his view of the credit depends on that connection.

responses.point: Lindroth wants a citation that credits magic-wavelength trapping and the 10^-18 level, while acknowledging that Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lisdat, PTB and NIST groups are excluded by a two-name prize.
responses.response: I take her wording over my round-1 citation, which named neither the accuracy level nor Ye's contribution to it. My new citation combines the two: invention through magic-wavelength trapping, realization at 10^-18. I do not think we should add a third name to cover the lattice-clock groups, because none of them is as clearly separable as Katori's proposal, and a larger set would blur the concept I regard as the centre of the credit. I agree with her that the disciplinary bias she flags as an atomic theorist is worth stating, and as a microscopist I weigh the experimental maturity of the result rather than the underlying atomic physics, so I am not in a position to judge the finer points of systematic uncertainty and rely on the cross-laboratory agreement.

responses.point: Eriksson says B009 would drop if the committee prefers a change in what physicists can think about over what they can measure, since B018 and B010 opened new fields while the clock sharpens a measurement.
responses.response: I understand the distinction, but the history of experimental physics supports both. A lattice clock changes what can be measured with a given system and it also introduced a many-body regime of clock operation that was not anticipated. I do not think a better measurement is a lesser achievement than a new concept when the measurement requires a new principle. I would therefore not drop B009 on that ground alone, and I note that Eriksson himself says the payoff has been delivered, which counts in its favour against B018, where the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang omissions leave a real credit question under the three-name limit.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats a magic-wavelength lattice as a new principle or as precision metrology close to 2005 and 2012; my confidence that it is a principle is moderate rather than high.
Whether a two-name citation can carry the narrower claim without implying that other lattice-clock groups contributed less than their milestones warrant.
How much the redefinition of the second should count for timing; I judge it irrelevant to the physics but cannot rule out that the committee prefers to wait.

Whether the committee can resolve credit among Halzen, Karle and Spiering, and relative to AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND, for B052; this would change my alternatives, though I doubt it would change my first choice.
My view of finer points of clock systematics and priority rests on recollection and on what colleagues reported in round 1; I have not verified them.
statement.conflict_note: I ranked B017 (aberration-corrected electron optics) first in my opening ballot. It lies in my own field of transmission electron microscopy, and I am reported as president of the International Federation of Societies for Microscopy in 2024, so I could be seen as having a professional stake. I have dropped B017 from my alternatives in this round, and I would accept recusal from any decision concerning it. Göran Johansson is a Chalmers colleague, which I disclose for transparency. I know of no connection to Katori, Ye or the other credited names on the shortlist, and I do not see a conflict in the B009 decision.
